utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you both. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with Barbara Baruch, we are assisted by Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. What's the bad news this morning, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is and it isn't. It is bad news in one sense. The witness -- do Your Honours have the witness list with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. One moment, until I dig it up. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness for this Friday is ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That much we know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And unable to travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's Witness 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.72, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the suggestion that we have, and it's really a matter for Your Honours and the Defence, although we wanted to call Mr. Sebire immediately after the Whit holiday because it meant not keeping a witness here very long we can put him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.44, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Nicolas Sebire. Does he have a number? 7.44. We would be able to deal with the exhumations. If Your Honours were content with that and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will bring -- Mr. Sebire has to come from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he's a member of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. With us, it's perfect. We are here available any way. So -- and if we are dealing with exhumations it shouldn't be a problem with you either, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I really couldn't -- [Microphone not activated] I must discuss that with Mr. Ackerman. If the Court is confident that it's not going to be a problem, I see no reason why it would be, but I have to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I will give you all the time in the world to do that. So let's do two things in the meantime. First alert Mr. Sebire if he hasn't been alerted already to be prepared just in case. Secondly, I don't have a statement from Nicolas Sebire to my knowledge. I don't know, perhaps Ms. Gustin can check that for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you probably don't at this stage because it's a sudden --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen anything for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour what we will do is try and make arrangements that Your Honours get it today or at the latest tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because it will also assist me and my colleague, Judge Janu to decide whether we should put some pressure on Defence or not, because if it's obvious that they need time, they require time, then we will give them time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what Mr. Sebire has done is -- he's an investigator and he has simply collated all the information that we have received which is still coming in, I may add, it's a never-lending saga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The results of exhumations carried out both under the aegis of the Tribunal itself or by the Bosnians and the declarations of death issued by the cantonal courts. Your Honour may remember you had some evidence about that from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had several witnesses giving details, particularly the Judge from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So but Your Honour that's the situation. Your Honour, that's that problem then hopefully dealt with. In respect of next Friday, the witness there cannot attend but we have done a swap with the witness for Friday the 13th. They both come from Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? You mean that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In other words, the witness for the 13th of Friday, I'm sorry, I haven't got the numbers on my form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are -- I suppose it's 7.102?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin will confirm that in a moment but it's a direct swap of the two Fridays, the witnesses for the two Fridays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words the one we should have had this Friday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, Friday week, that is, the 6th of June, the one who should have come on the 13th will come on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 7.67 will go to the 13th? And 7.102 will go to the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It should be like -- 7.67 will be shifted to the 13th? And 7.102 to the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing I would like you to confirm is that these two numbers are correct, 7.67, 7.102 so that the Defence will know exactly what they should be prepared for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? Which witness to cross-examine, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will just confirm all that at the break with the Defence and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also what is important is that all documents that need to be in the hands of the Defence, particularly with regard to 7.102, because we are two weeks afar from that, are in the hands of the Defence by the end of this week already early next week at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I leave it with you -- I leave that in your hands. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I before I deal with Mr. Ackerman -- the matters Your Honour has raised yesterday at the end of the day can I just go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour raised yesterday Mr. Ackerman's reply to the motion in respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I raised it in order to avoid you having to file a further response to the response. We will deal with it orally and then my legal secretary who is here present should be -- would be in a position to move ahead once I have directed her where to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this is the motion in respect of the Rule 92 witnesses for Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll come on to the documents. If Your Honours have got it there, paragraph 2 with regard to witnesses, he's made an error in the number it should be 7.148, not 7.48. 7.149 and 7.115. All these witnesses are victims of rape. It was originally intended to call 7.115 and have the other two as cumulative of that witness. Because of the indications that we've had from Your Honours that you really would wish us if at all possible to finish the case by the adjournment in August, which is the 1st of August, we took a decision that as there has been no cross-examination at all effectively of any of the people who said that they were the victims of rape, that we would seek to Rule 92 them. I have no idea what Rule 93 bis is because it doesn't exist. And therefore I'm assuming that Mr. Ackerman, it's a typing error again, it should be 92 bis and he's saying that although they are not cumulative of a live witness he actually has no objection and in each case we do have the Rule 92 attestations. So if that's right, Your Honour, I would invite Your Honour that these may be tendered if Mr. Ackerman has no objection in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In actual fact, that's what he says also in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I have no authority to speak for him so perhaps you will make a note of it and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I've already discussed it with him and he does not have an objection for it being 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So that answers the only problem that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents. I'm not sure what Your Honour wanted me to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I am trying to avoid you having to file a response to this objection, if you can deal with it orally here and now, on your two feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can. Your Honour, I'm going to say the same thing I have said over and over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is not -- none of these objections, we suggest, really raise anything -- with one exception. I had a look at the list and I think there is another one of those documents that we can't trace a source for. If Your Honour just waits a moment while I -- in actual fact, funnily enough, it's not one that's objected to by Mr. Ackerman. Your Honour, it's P1738. It's the same source, if you see what I mean, it's the same gentleman who collected the other four documents that were in the Prnjavor binder -- no, Petrovac binder, where we couldn't trace from the documentation where he got them from. Mr. Inayat is still trying to chase it up but it's actually quite difficult because it was so long ago that this gentleman was dealing with matters that in the absence of having documentation to show where it comes from, it's quite difficult but Mr. Inayat is seeing if he can trace it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, in respect of the other objections, Your Honour, we would invite Your Honour to admit the whole of the Teslic binder of documents, Mr. Ackerman's objections notwithstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mrs. Baruch, we will not hand down a written decision on this. We will just give an oral decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I just understand? Because I'm looking at a document that was the objection, there were objections, clear objections, to three documents: P1937, a press report that came off of Croatian Radio; P1940, which although it says it had no signature, there was a signature but there was no stamp, that came from AID; and P1950, again a press report and I believe that's also from Croatian Radio. Those are the three documents I believe that Mr. Ackerman actually objected to, and then asked the Court to examine many of the other documents in depth. That's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, until now, as of now, I haven't seen actually these three documents that are being objected to. I will see them in the course of the day when they are made available to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour not have the Teslic binder? Because I'm going to be using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think we have the Teslic binder but I haven't had them pulled out and shown to me and this is the problem. Yesterday I was here until 7.30. After the sitting, there was a meeting of Trial Chamber II so there was little time after that to go and examine any documents, Ms. Korner, so after ten hours straight here. I'll see, together with Judge Janu, these three documents and we will reach a decision probably later on today, okay? Okay. Probably later on today. In the meantime Inneke, please, liaise with Rene so that they are on my desk during the first break. So ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, one last piece of news. I see Mrs. Baruch is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, after he'd finished testifying I spoke to him just to thank him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me a protected witness? No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I spoke to him just to thank him for coming to the Court. He then informed me that back at his hotel, he had other documents. I then made arrangements for an investigator and an interpreter to go over to the hotel and collect from him any documents that were relevant to any of these matters. Some of them were. Your Honour, I can't say anything other than we are very sorry. We didn't appreciate -- he was asked to bring the documents that you remember we had to get translated overnight, and it may be that we didn't make ourselves clear enough that we didn't just mean the documents that supported his notebook but any other documents that he might have. We have arranged that they will be -- we hope the B/C/S versions will be given, disclosed today. We are making -- we hope so. We just have to get it together. We are trying to make arrangements again for a rather quicker translation than can be done by CLSS so that they will be available at the end of the week because there is another witness from the same municipality, Petrovac, who will be here on Monday. Your Honour, of course, if there are matters that the Defence wish to cross-examine about, then we will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. make arrangements if necessary though we hope it won't be necessary because of the expense, for Mr. Hidic to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Baruch? Or Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I won't know if there is additional cross-examination required until I see the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The position as I see it from a legal point of view, from a procedural point of view, ought to be the following: First of all, I reserve for the Defence the right, after having perused these documents, to ask for Mr. Hidic to be brought over for any possible cross-examination. And that would also mean that the Prosecution would be entitled to put questions to him as well. In the meantime, however, I would require that simultaneous with the filing of these documents, whoever received them or picked them up from Mr. Hidic, to be brought forward and confirm that on oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's made a statement, Your Honour. We appreciated what might happen and so the investigator has made a statement as to the events and the documents that he took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So I have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't proposing to file, unless Your Honour wants it filed. I was proposing to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Filing is a matter of saying. Before being made use of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before being tendered in evidence as exhibits, that's important, because, I mean, we need to establish the origin. It's not that I doubt your word. Don't take me -- it's a formality that probably we need to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I did ask that in this case, we keep, just for the time being, the originals which are, I'm told, very similar to the ones he produced himself in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, incidentally, Nicolas Sebire on Friday, how long do you expect him to be in the witness stand?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't really know. It depends on how much, A, the Defence want to ask him about his collation of documents, and B, there are a number of schedules that he's going to be producing. I would have thought a bit like Mr. Kaiser, that it should be possible to finish him within the one day but I wouldn't like to bet on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have difficulties particularly, Mr. Cunningham and Mrs. Baruch, we are talking of schedules and details which you may not be familiar with and which you need to go through considering that this witness is here available at any time, we could actually do the in-chief on Friday and reserve the cross-examination for you for some later point in time, if you prefer it. If you think you are -- you will be in a position to conclude also with the cross-examination on Friday, then we conclude it on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are perfectly content with that because, as I say, we had actually originally arranged for him to testify on the Tuesday after the bank -- the Whitsun holiday, so we could reserve cross-examination for them which would help maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All we could ask is an opportunity to confer with Mr. Ackerman and report back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We are flexible, Mr. Cunningham, so you don't have to worry on that. So shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, did you get the message that next week we will be working in the morning and not in the afternoon? We have shifted all the sittings from the afternoon to the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't, Your Honour, but I imagine so because I know how few cases are going to be sitting next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And will it be in this Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That much I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought they were finishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Simic had the last sitting yesterday, I think. No? In any case, it's an advantage even for Mr. Ackerman himself to sit in the morning rather than stay here until 7.00 in the evening. All right. Witness? Does he enjoy any protective --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he doesn't, Your Honour. Did Your Honour get -- I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The briefing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The extra statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- simply where he'd made corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I simply don't -- I got them and they are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to give evidence and testimony. Before you do so, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, a formula with which I am sure you are familiar, and I suggest you take in your hand the text of the solemn declaration and go ahead by reading it aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Now, what's going to happen, Mr. Osmanovic, is that you are going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Korner, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, a case which has been instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin, and she will then be followed by the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin on cross-examination. It may well be that you will not finish your testimony today. In other words, that you will -- we may have to continue tomorrow. We will try to do our best to have you finish your testimony tomorrow, but I can't promise that. Very much depends on how you answer the questions. Many witnesses have the habit of giving us more information than they are asked for. So my suggestion to you is to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question, and I can assure you that if you do that, you will leave this Tribunal earlier than you think. So Ms. Korner, he is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you be very kind and give us your name.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Adil Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 24th of July, 1963?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Bosniak by nationality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you presently president of the regional SDA board for Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But are you presently, therefore, a vice-president of the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not the assembly, but Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which shows the folly of trying to lead. Were you, however, when your statement was taken in 2000, the president of the regional SDA board?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did you become the vice-president of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last general elections, in October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Up until May of 1992, from the time of the multi-party elections, were you a member of the SDA in Teslic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If I can deal briefly with your background, I think that you attended, after your secondary education in Sarajevo, an arts and language facility in Pristina between 1984 and 1990.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With a two-year break for your JNA military service?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after graduating for Pristina, did you go to a village called Hrankovic in the Teslic municipality where you performed religious services as an imam at the mosque there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you hold that position between January, 1990 and the 1st of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then after the multi-party elections, in April of 1991, did you -- were you appointed to the position of secretary to the municipal assembly for the Teslic municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you first of all, please, a little bit about Teslic and then deal with your position. Could you have a look, please, at the census document for 1991? It's Exhibit P60. And if you can find Teslic, which, I think, you will find on the last page but one.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that in 1991, the total population of Teslic was just under 60.000 people, 59.854?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the Croats were some 9.525, forming 15.9 per cent. The Muslims 12.802, 21 per cent, and then the Serbs, 32.962, 55.1 per cent. And then a few people who declared themselves Yugoslavs or others. So Teslic -- in Teslic there was an overall majority of Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think we need to look now please at a map of Bosnia to identify the whereabouts of Teslic rather than the ARK map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a new map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, let me ask him a question. I notice from this table that you were just looking at, that over the space of -- a period of 20 years, that's from 1971 to 1991, the population, the Serb component of the population, was on the decline, it was 62 per cent -- 62 per cent in 1971, at 32.700, it went up to 35.000 in 1981, dropped back to 32, which is equivalent to 55 per cent, as against the 62 per cent that it was 20 years earlier. Can you fathom a reason for this? Do you have an idea why this could be so? Why the Serb population was diminishing in a municipality which was predominantly Serb?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this witness was not in that town at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but perhaps he knows. Let's see whether he can give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that during the 1971 census period, a significant number of Muslims declared themselves differently. They didn't declare themselves as Muslims, and also a significant number of Serbs worked in Vojvodina and in Serbia, so there was a migration of population within the then Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough for the time being. Yes. Ms. Korner, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all we need to do with that document. Could you be handed now, please, a map of the whole of Bosnia? There are copies available for Your Honours because I don't think we've used this one before. And if we could put it up on the ELMO? Sir, you'll be able to see it on the screen in front of you. Except it's upside down, usher. All right. Can we see on that map -- I don't know whether we can focus a little bit better on it, yeah, we need -- usher if you could pull -- we need the left hand bit to come -- no, sorry, the other way, and down, no, down. Thank you. That's great. We can see there, if we see Doboj at the right-hand side of the screen, we can see Teslic just below that as we are looking at it, to the left, and then the road to Banja Luka, and we can see, I think, that going up from Doboj to Derventa and then we see the Croatian border, do we?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Roughly -- I'm sorry, you've taken Teslic off. The focus -- sorry, the focus is too -- I want Teslic. Thanks. Stop, that's it. Roughly how far was Teslic from the border of Croatia that we can see, Bosanski Brod and up there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Around 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just for the purposes of this -- can we focus on the left-hand side of the map as we look at it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't have this map when the Petrovac witness was here but Your Honours will see rather more clearly than with the ARK map Petrovac to the left there and then we can see down the side of that Drvar and Knin is just over -- can we pull the map slightly to the right? No. Can we see it? No. We can see Bihac at the top. Never mind. Anyhow, that's what I wanted to do. Your Honours have the map in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour, that will be 1956, please. We've jumped some numbers because of the Rule 92 statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next, can I ask you to look at a map that deals with the ethnicity, the nationality of the various areas?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't at the moment got any other copies, they are going to be brought down so perhaps I can put it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see there -- and I think you've had a chance to look at it, and can you confirm that the villages shown in green had a Muslim majority within those villages and areas? And would you agree that that's pretty accurate?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The green colour indeed shows those areas where Muslims were a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 1992, is this where they were a majority?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see Teslic town itself is marked as largely Serb but there is a particular area called Stenjak where there were Muslims; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you yourself live in the Stenjak area?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up to 1992, I lived in Stenjak. That was up to the end of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just jump ahead to the present time, 2003? Would that map be an accurate description of the way the ethnicities were split? Are Gornji Rankovic, Gornji Teslic, places like that, are they still a Muslim majority?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't have any accurate figures but roughly how many Muslims are living presently in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Teslic the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can answer the question. If you can't, say so.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise number, but I can give you a rough estimate because I was until recently a deputy in the Municipal Assembly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of Teslic, so the number would be between 4 and a half and 5.000 Bosniaks who currently reside in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that map. And then that would be P1957, please. And finally, I want you to look at a map with some photographs. Are you able, on the left-hand -- can we move the thing so we can see the photographs on the left of the -- thank you. Are you able to identify photograph number 3 on that map? Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: On that photograph, you can see clearly the building which housed the political and social associations which made part of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic up to June, 1992. On the left-hand side, but you can't see it on this photo is the public security station, the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say the political parties. Did all the political parties have their offices in this one building? Political associations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the general elections which took place in November, 1992, when the administration in Teslic was founded, all the political parties which had their seats in the municipal assembly had their offices in this room. That meant the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, and then existing the Socialist Democratic Alliance, the Alliance of Reformists and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was translated 1992. Did you mean to say 1992? Don't worry, Ms. Baruch, I can see these things myself.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. After the general elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the first elections that ever took place in the former Yugoslavia. That is the multi-party elections when the administration was established in Teslic, then all the political parties got room for offices in this building and they kept those offices up to mid-May or late May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the only other photograph, could you look at, please, photograph number 5, which is on the right-hand side? Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This building housed the Territorial Defence staff and the Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was the municipal building? Can we see that in any of the photographs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal building -- you can't see it on this photo but it was not far from this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From the TO building?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not far from the Territorial Defence staff building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will then become P1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we go back to your job in the municipal assembly? You were appointed as the secretary of the municipal assembly. After the election, did the -- was the SDS in control approximately of 48 per cent of the assembly? In other words, they had 48 per cent of the seats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so did they hold the key positions in the assembly, namely the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The president and -- of the assembly and the president of the executive board came from their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the president of the assembly a gentleman named Nikola Peresic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the president of the executive board Milorad Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did the SDS, i.e., the Serbs, also have charge of the Territorial Defence unit, the commander being a gentleman named Cedo Grbic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the chief of police also a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that a gentleman named Dusan Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that the SDA had 16 per cent of the seats, and did they hold the following positions: The vice-president of the executive board, who was a Mr. Mahalbasic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ferid Mahalbasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also the secretary to the Secretariat of the People's Defence? Was that a gentleman named Mensur Degirmendzic? You tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mensur Degirmendzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yourself as secretary to the assembly. And then finally, the HDZ, the Croatian party, did that have 10 per cent of the seats and they held a few positions, though not particularly high ones?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, please, a little bit about first of all your position as secretary and your duties. What were the duties of the secretary to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The secretary to the assembly had to look after the legality of the work of the municipal assembly. He was also the first assistant to the president of the assembly when it came to preparing the upcoming sessions of the assembly. All the documents, all the materials, that were to be discussed by the municipal assembly would be prepared by the various heads of the Secretariats, and then they would forward them to the secretary to the assembly, at which stage the secretary, together with the president of the municipal assembly, would prepare the agenda of the upcoming session of the assembly and that would be the final preparation for the upcoming session of the assembly. So that would be in a nutshell what the role of the secretary was, and that is exactly what I did in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were your duties actually defined by law, by the Statute of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the preparation of the agenda which you did with the president of the assembly, was that an important matter?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, according to the statute and the book of rules that governed the work of the assembly, the president was in charge of proposing an agenda to the municipal assembly, so he was authorised by the statute to propose the agenda, and the topics to be discussed by the deputies largely depended on the decision of the president, and hence all the decisions that were to be made by the assembly depend on the president. Certainly the last say on that was by the assembly but the proposal was up to the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What would have to happen if the deputies to the assembly wanted to alter the agenda in some way?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the session of the assembly, the president would put forward the agenda for discussion and every deputy was in the position to either remove certain items from the agenda or alternatively, to propose some new items to be added to the agenda, in providing that the relevant Secretariat had enough time to prepare the required materials for the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And would there have to be a vote in the assembly as to whether or not a particular item would be added to the agenda?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first vote was on those proposals, and if those proposals received a qualified majority, then they would be added to the finalised agenda for that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the president could set the agenda himself without any vote, but if somebody wanted something added, there would have to be a vote?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to jump forward for a moment to the time after you'd left Teslic and you were in Tesanj and were placed in charge of a Crisis Staff that was set up, or War Presidency, I should say, in exile. Appreciating that you had no -- nothing to control, as it were, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because you were in exile, but would the same procedures about the setting of the agenda by the president of the Crisis Staff in consultation with his secretary, be followed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, once the agenda was set and matters were discussed, if a decision had to be made, how would that decision be taken?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm returning to the assembly. You've told us about the agenda, the items on the agenda. If there had to be a decision made, for example as to the distribution of oil, how would that decision be arrived at in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If a decision were to be adopted, if it would really be on the agenda, and if this kind of decision were adopted by a parliamentary majority, then it would enter into force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the actual mechanics. You say a parliamentary majority. Would there be a vote?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a vote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the majority decided either in favour or against, was that then a binding decision? Or could the --

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That decision is binding. If it is passed by a qualified majority in the assembly, the kind of majority required to pass a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the president of the assembly have any power to overrule a decision made by the members of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If, during the actual vote, the president were to vote against a draft decision, and if the parliamentary majority were to be in favour of that decision, it is the duty of the president to see that the decision is implemented nevertheless, even if he were against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And once a decision was taken, did it have to be signed by the president, if he was present, before it could become law?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the president presides over the assembly, it is his duty to sign all the decisions that are passed by the assembly, and then these decisions are published in the Official Gazette of the assembly of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And would they come into effect, the decisions, before they were published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was only the publication in the gazette, was it, that gave those decisions the force of law, effectively that what was decided could take place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of every decision, it says that it shall enter into force on its date of publication in the Official Gazette of the municipality, or at the end of some other decisions it may say that they shall enter into force within a certain time period, within 30 days or 60 days but they have to be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Supposing the president was absent from an assembly meeting, was anybody else authorised to sign these decisions in his absence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Decisions that are passed by the assembly are signed by the person who had chaired the assembly meeting. If the president was not in a position to chair the actual meeting, if he were replaced by the vice-president of the assembly, then it would be the vice-president who would sign the decision concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally I want to ask you briefly, please, about the executive council of the assembly. What was its function?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the setup of the municipalities as they existed then, we also had an executive board which could be called a local government or a municipal government. The executive board was in charge of preparing bills that were to become laws. Then these bills would be submitted to the president in order for them to appear on the agenda. The executive board consisted of secretaries of the Secretariats. Then there were two people from the outside so to speak, volunteers, who covered specific areas like the economy, for instance. The executive board as the word itself says, is an executive body. It is in charge of implementing the decisions that were adopted by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it report to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are appointed by the assembly and the assembly possibly relieves them of their duties as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we turn to your relationship with Mr. Peresic, who was the president of the assembly? Did you have -- what sort of a working relationship did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the establishment of the assembly and the executive government in Teslic, Mr. Peresic, the president of the assembly, and I had rather good and professional relations, until the beginning of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us that the president had to abide by the vote that was taken by the deputies, whether he agreed with it or not. In the case of Mr. Peresic, was he able in any way to affect decisions that were taken?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the assembly.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the president was the person who would propose the agenda for the meeting, so then he would have the -- he should have the political wisdom, if I can put it that way, not to put anything on the agenda that would not receive adequate support or rather majority support.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Supposing -- and I'm dealing specifically with Mr. Peresic now -- a decision was taken that he didn't like, was he able to do anything about it, if not directly, indirectly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we were to abide by the statute and legal enactments passed by the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, the president should not do anything against a decision that had been adopted by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. But what I'm asking is even if legally he had to abide by it, in reality, was he able to in some way affect a decision that had already been taken?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at given points in time, he certainly could, as the president, and as the person who exercises authority among the secretaries of the Secretariats of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how would he do that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that I have any information to that effect, that he had actually done such things, but as president he could call in the secretaries of the Secretariats and he could say that even if a decision were adopted, it would not have to be dealt with that seriously and it wouldn't have to be implemented to the letter. That would be sufficient for having the people who were supposed to carry out the decision have certain reservations about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, generally speaking, what were relationships like between the different nationalities up until the war in Croatia started?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the town of Teslic itself, in the municipality of Teslic, after the elections, the first democratic elections, in November 1990, when an entire system had been replaced, the communist system, that is, there was great delight among the citizens. Interethnic relations in Teslic, among all the ethnic groups, were indeed at a rather high level. That's the kind of atmosphere that prevailed in the assembly of the municipality of Teslic too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there -- had intermarriages between the nationalities, the ethnicities, taken place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in Teslic town itself, we've seen that Stenjak, you told us, where you lived, was a suburb, I think of the town and was a Muslim area. What about other areas? Were they segregated or mixed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The villages around Teslic were rather mono-ethnic but the town itself was truly multi-ethnic. Like all -- like in all towns in Bosnia, there were apartment buildings and members of different ethnic groups were neighbours within these buildings. They had apartments right next to each other. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, then, please, to the events after the war in Croatia began. When there was the call for mobilisation, did the Bosniaks or Muslims respond to the call?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that affect the relationships?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to a large degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in what way?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because Bosniaks and Croats did not respond to the mobilisation call-up because they were afraid that they would be sent to the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did -- did the Serbs respond to the mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did that affect the way that the Serbs treated the Croat and Muslim population in Teslic, in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a large number -- or rather there were quite a few Serbs who were volunteers, who took part in the war in Croatia, who were there at the front line, but then a large number were mobilised as well. A considerable number of Serbs from Teslic were killed in the battlefields in Croatia. All of this led to tensions in the relations between Serbs on the one hand and Bosniaks and Croats on the other hand. Also many soldiers who were returning from the front line and who had experienced everything that they had experienced there, bloodshed, suffering, et cetera, all of that certainly did affect their relationship with the Bosniak and Croat population in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to look, please, at the political alignment of where Teslic was. We can see that Teslic was close to Doboj and certainly closer to Doboj than to Banja Luka. Was there a link between Teslic and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was always a link between Teslic and Doboj, because these are two neighbouring towns relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In terms of the political area, in terms of finance and whatever, was Teslic aligned to Doboj or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, Teslic was always aligned to Doboj in terms of financial flows, and in terms of health care. People were sent for medical treatment to Doboj, to the hospital in Doboj, from the health centre in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During 1991, was there ever a proposal made that Teslic should be aligned to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By whom was that proposal made?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the regular session of the assembly, the president of the assembly acted in a rather unusual manner and just before the agenda was adopted, he suggested that the agenda should include the following, namely that the municipality of Teslic should be annexed to the Banja Luka region. Then the assemblymen started debating the issue. All the assemblymen from the ranks of other political parties except for the assemblymen coming from the Serb Democratic Party, were opposed to this, and then the president withdrew this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was there opposition from all parties save the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because there was not a single valid argument for Teslic being annexed to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the -- did Mr. Peresic explain why he and the other members of the SDS wished to join the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The president then presented the following argumentation: That the Banja Luka region is stronger economically and that in that context, the municipality of Teslic would fare better. That's what he said publicly. In the conversation that I had with him, this was a tete-a-tete conversation, he said that they were safer there in the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he explain what he meant by safer?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that area, in the broader area of the Banja Luka region, the SDS was in government, that is to say around the region, and therefore it was better for them than Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Doboj like, then, as an area, in the sense of who controlled it, which party?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from Teslic to -- between Teslic and Doboj, there was the municipality of Tesanj and the SDA was in government there. The municipality of Gracanica is right next to Doboj, again the Party of Democratic Action was in power there and in Doboj itself the SDA and the SDS were more or less equally in control. The president of the municipal assembly in Doboj was from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this topic, can you remember roughly when this proposal was made by Mr. Peresic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you heard at all of something called the association of Bosnian Krajina municipalities? I think I'm mixing it slightly but something like that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that in existence at the time that Mr. Peresic made the proposal?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to a new topic so perhaps that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. We will have a 25-minute break so that means resuming at roughly 5 to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we were talking about the attempt that was made to join the Banja Luka region. At around this time, did you notice any change in your relationship with your -- or rather your dealings professionally with Mr. Peresic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the change?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Up to then, we had regular meetings, we had regular contacts, and exchanges of views and opinions. We cooperated in preparing the upcoming sessions of the assembly. After that period, however, I noticed that the relationship between me and the president of the assembly was no longer at a professional level. I also noticed that he was prone to organise meetings with the secretaries of Secretariats only, and only those who were Serbs. His contacts with the chief of the Public Security Station of Teslic were also more frequent than before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you discover about meetings he was holding with other presidents of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From whom did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I received this information regarding the presidents of municipal assemblies who were Serbs holding meetings on the territories of particular municipalities. I received this information from many friends and the most striking information to that effect was from the secretary for People's Defence, Mr. Mensur Degirmendzic, who had received a fax that was addressed to his office. In that fax, a meeting of the Serbian presidents of municipal assemblies was called and, by mistake, it reached his office rather than some other office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to then move through the remainder of the events of 1991, and I don't think there is any dispute about the fact that in late August, early September, the JNA took over the records and files of the military reservists from the Secretariat of the People's Defence. What was the importance of that, as far as Teslic was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In late August or early September, officers of the JNA arrived in Teslic. Their task was to take over all the records from the Secretariat of People's Defence and place them under their control. The importance of those records lies primarily in the fact that those records contained all the data, all the particulars, of all the reserve officers and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. establishment of all the units. If one has these records, then one can carry out a mobilisation within the space of 24 hours and end up with all the exact establishment of all the units along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, was the matter of the taking over of these records by the JNA discussed in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: What surprised me and many others was the fact that we never carried out any sort of discussion about this problem at any of the sessions of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, although everybody was aware of the fact that civilians in Teslic opposed to the JNA taking over those records. There was a rally which almost escalated into an incident. However, this was never discussed at any of the sessions of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But did you discuss the matter personally with Mr. Peresic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I told him that such a move on the part of the JNA is something that I could not understand and that I could not accept. He simply told me that the JNA was the only armed force on the territory of Yugoslavia which was a legitimate armed force and that it had the authority that it had. I could not agree with that, because at that time we did not need a military administration, and everybody pointed into that direction. I also told him that I could no longer perceive the JNA as the army of all the peoples and of all the nationalities that existed on the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that? Why had your view of the JNA changed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The developments that took place on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the moves on the part of the high ranking officers of the JNA who communicated only with representatives of the Serbian people, pointed to the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army was the army of only one people, and increasingly an army of just one political party, and that was the Serbian democratic party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did the JNA in fact come to Teslic and take the records?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. After this very hard day when a number of civilians wanted to prevent the JNA from taking those records from the Secretariat, many of those civilians literally placed their bodies in front of the vehicles of the JNA to prevent this from happening. The JNA, i.e., its officers, withdrew but on the following night, when the duty officer in the Secretariat was a Serbian citizen, they got in the building and they took all the records that they wanted to take on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, up until the autumn of 1991, were there any JNA units stationed in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that change in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In a very strange way. An active officer of the JNA, whose family name was -- I can't remember exactly, he came to talk with the president of the municipal assembly. We found out that in the village of Djulici where certain facilities of the JNA were at the time, a JNA unit was stationed there. This unit was some 100 men strong. And this was the first time ever that active officers of the JNA and its troop were present in Teslic or in its immediate vicinity, because this village of Djulici was in the immediate vicinity of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that you couldn't remember the family name of the officer. Were you able to remember it at the time you made your statement to the investigator in 2000?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that he was then replaced by Dejan Bilanovic but currently I can't remember the name of this first person, the person that Mr. Dejan Bilanovic replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a -- unless there is an objection I mean, I can either lead it from him from his statement or ask him to refresh his memory from his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, you can go ahead. I wouldn't imagine there is a strong objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the name of the first officer Major Veljko Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that he met with the president of the municipality. Did you -- were you ever given an explanation by Mr. Peresic as to why this JNA unit was suddenly being stationed there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was any kind of training being carried out within the municipality by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was that being carried out?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, we received information from some of the citizens of Teslic municipality who moved about the entire territory of the municipality for various reasons, either for farm work or some other reasons, and they told us that a number of the troops of the JNA were stationed in a Serbian village called Jesenova and that in that area, there was an intensive training of reservists taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again, around this period of time, the autumn of 1991, was there anything happening in relation to non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that? First of all, what kind of property? Private or commercial?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Private property, the property belonging to Bosniaks and Croats, of those who had already been targeted in summer and autumn of 1992, their property was blown up or set fire to. The property that I'm talking about, are mostly summer cottages that were not permanently inhabited by their owners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The translation of what you said is that they were targeted in the summer and autumn of 1992. Did you mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: 1991. I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were these explosions or arson investigated by the police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the police did carry out some on-site investigations but without any results. All they did was to make a note of the act but perpetrators were never found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move through quickly the last real event of 1991. Did the Serbs hold a plebiscite in November of 1991 in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: A plebiscite did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in -- moving through until early 1992, was there then the referendum in February, organised by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want, before I deal with the last part of the events that you were concerned with in Teslic, to ask you about the Autonomous Region of Krajina so-called. Did you become aware of the creation of such an autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware? From the media or from any other information that you were given?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of the Serbs creating something called the Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Also from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn whether Mr. Peresic had anything to do with this particular autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever meet Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of Mr. Brdjanin? And can you tell us, if you did, when you first became aware of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Brdjanin -- actually, I became aware of him through the electronic and written media. I never saw him personally face to face. It is only today that I'm seeing him for the first time. I know that he was a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I saw him in the media, I read about him, and I followed his appearances and activities, but only through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want me to ask him to identify him Mr. Brdjanin, as he said he saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned and he also said that he's seen him here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's just stated that he's seeing him for the first time today. Perhaps he may look left, right and centre and identify him for us, if he can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed since the last in-court identification that the acknowledgement of the various common law countries and authorities followed by this Court is that the setup in the courtroom is so prejudicial and influential with regard to such identifications, that it would be inappropriate to do so in the courtroom and for that reason, I am objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not -- the objection is not sustained. It's overruled. It's only because the witness has pointed out that he is seeing him here for the first time that we want to make sure that he is seeing the right person. So otherwise, we wouldn't have asked him to identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just -- the best thing would be if you can look around the Court and tell us whether you can see Mr. Brdjanin and if so, where.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see him to the left side of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there anybody next to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose technically I see my last words because I muttered them, for the record that he identified Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know it's a long time ago, sir, but can you remember now anything about the sort of speeches that Mr. Brdjanin was making?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Brdjanin, at least during the period while I followed the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when he spoke in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, his political speeches were rather heated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you give us a little bit more detail of that? What do you mean by "rather heated"?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "heated," I mean that the discussions in the parliament regarding the referendum, he was the advocate of the Serbs living in Yugoslavia and he said that the Serbs would never accept the independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally on Mr. Brdjanin, did you become aware of his position -- I'm sorry, I should go back. Did you become aware of the establishment of a regional Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region with its base in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, how did you hear about that? Through the media or through people telling you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you become aware, again, obviously, through the media, of Mr. Brdjanin's position on that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that position was what?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, after the referendum that took place on the independence of Bosnia, how did that affect the Assembly in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This had a huge bearing, a huge negative bearing on the work of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic. The plebiscite was carried out, the so-called by the election commission of the municipality of Teslic which consisted of Serbs only, and the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was carried out by the legitimate municipal election commission that existed in Teslic. Moreover, the Municipal Assembly of Teslic no longer had the correct harmony amongst the political parties that existed before, and there was a deterioration in the professional relationship between the president of the municipal assembly and the president of the executive board on the one hand, and the secretary to the municipal assembly on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when there was a meeting of the assembly to discuss joining the Teslic municipality to the Serbian republic, which had been declared?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that meeting attended by all the deputies?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I as the secretary to the assembly, the secretaries of various Secretariats, or any of the deputies from the Croatian or Muslim peoples were not aware of such assembly session being prepared, nor did we ever found out when it took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you get to hear about it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of April, 1991, the president of the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, Mr. Milorad Markovic, called all the secretaries of the Secretariats of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic to a meeting. At that meeting, he told us that on the previous day, there had been a session of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic and that at that session, a decision had been made for municipality of Teslic to join the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The present officials belonging to the Bosniak and Croat peoples found this very surprising.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said again or it's the translation, in the first half of April, 1991. Can we take it you meant 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look, please, at a document, Exhibit P1921.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening can I correct an exhibit number that I gave to Your Honour on the maps, just so it's there? The ethnic map should have been P1958, not P1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: , I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have the ethnic map originally as 1957 and -- A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. The -- what was 1959 does not have -- is not the ethnic map but it's the map with some corresponding photos. So that I assume needs to become 1958 because there was no 1958 in between the 1959 and the 1957. So the ethnic map would, I assume, remain 1957.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm sorry, there was a slight confusion over maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's not the first time that that happens, Ms. Korner. So ... yesterday, we had a hell of a confusion in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think, sir, you saw that until you arrived at this Court to look at these documents; is that correct? You didn't see Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will just go through it and then I want to ask you something about it. It is allegedly -- and it's signed you apparently by Mr. Peresic. Do you recognise the signature of Mr. Peresic?.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is the formal document that states that the Teslic Municipal Assembly at the meeting held on the 6th of April, adopted by a majority vote, the following decision: "Teslic a constituent part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, of the territory of the Serbian republic, that the constitution and laws of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall become null and void, and laws of the Serbian republic applied."
