And then to deal with the administrative organs, "pending final consolidation of the Serbian autonomous region of Northern Bosnia, all functions of municipal administrative organs and state and public institutions shall be performed through the organs of the autonomous region of the Bosnian Krajina whose seat is in Banja Luka." And then a call for the citizens to accept this, particularly the Muslim and Croatian fellow citizens. Now, the form of this document, did that comply with the normal form of documents issuing decisions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What should it -- what should this document have contained?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was done rather unprofessionally. All documents that were adopted by the Municipal Assembly of Teslic had a preamble that was quite different. In the preamble, it would say that pursuant to article such and such of the statute of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, and pursuant to such and such article of the rules of procedure of the municipality -- Municipal Assembly of Teslic, at a regular session, and then there should be the number of that session, whether it was the 5th session or the 15th session, et cetera, the following decision has been passed. It never said by a majority vote, because by mentioning the rules of procedure in the preamble, it was obvious that any decision that was passed meant that it was passed by majority vote. Since this document was drafted in this way, it should have invoked this so-called constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and such and such an article should have been mentioned again, the rules of procedure of the Municipal Assembly of Teslic should have been mentioned too, because it was still in force. Also, it should be noted then that such and such a decision was passed, item 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, but this shows that this document or this decision does not refer to any valid document. The Statute of the municipal assembly or the rules of procedure of the municipal assembly, or the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before this decision to join the Serb republic, had there been any discussions between yourself and Mr. Peresic or the SDA and the SDS about splitting the assembly into a Serbian assembly and a non-Serb assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, you -- you can take the document, thank you very much. You were telling us how you were informed by Mr. Markovic about the decision that had been taken. Did Mr. Markovic explain to you what you had -- what you and the other members of the assembly had to do if you wanted to continue to work?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After having informed us of the fact that a decision was passed on the annexation of the municipality of Teslic to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Milorad Markovic said that all the employees of the municipality, notably elected officials, if they wished to remain in their positions, should state -- should sign, rather, statements of allegiance to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were all truly surprised by this kind of thing. I said that none of the officials that were proposed by the Party of Democratic Action to certain positions in the municipal assembly would not sign such an illegal, illegitimate and unnecessary allegiance to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that this is indeed an unconstitutional and unlawful way for the assembly to work, as well as for the president of the executive board, and I also said that professional staff members employed in the assembly or municipal organs of Teslic should at least be spared from signing these statements of allegiance to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We elected officials came to our positions from certain jobs that we had held previously so we can simply go to our original jobs, whereas people who were staff members at the municipal assembly for 15 or 20 years had no where else to go if they would not sign this statement of allegiance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Markovic's reaction to what you said to him? What did he tell you would happen if people didn't sign?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic wanted to show his principled stance and rigid stance vis-a-vis this decision passed by the Municipal Assembly of Teslic and he said that all of those who didn't sign this statement of allegiance to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain jobless regardless of whether they were elected officials or professional staff within the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to people who didn't sign the loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Neither I nor other officials belonging to the Muslim and Croat peoples, did not sign this loyalty oath, and this period went on until the second half of April. Afterwards, people were dismissed if they did not sign this loyalty oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We got a double negative in this. So do you mean that you and the other officials didn't sign?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We did not. We did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were dismissed eventually and others. What about people such as the police? Were there any non-Serbs in the police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, this loyalty oath came to apply to the police and public services. First it focused on the municipality and the police, and all of those who did not sign it remained jobless.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, around this time, April of 1992, were checkpoints set up?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, checkpoints were already being established in Teslic vis-a-vis neighbouring municipalities and vis-a-vis villages where there were Muslims and Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was manning the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: These checkpoints were manned by unknown men. We called them paramilitary formations. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever discover if these paramilitary formations had any kind of name?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at one other document, P1925. I'm not sure I made the last one an exhibit. Did I? Oh, it's already. I'm crazy, it's already got a number. Could we have a look at P1925, please? Now, this is a document which is headed the Teslic municipality Crisis Staff, and it's dated the 6th of May. Did you know before you left at the end of May, Teslic, that there was now a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you find out about it? Did somebody tell you about it or did you hear about it on the media?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it directly from some of my friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Peresic tell you that a Crisis Staff was established, of which he was now the head, president?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look, please, at item 1.8, that states that all paramilitary formations and individuals illegally possessing arms and ammunition are called upon to hand them over to the municipal TO staff or the nearest military unit immediately or by no later than 1500 hours on 11 May, 1992. After the expiry of this deadline, responsible organs will search and confiscate arms and ammunition applying the most rigorous sanctions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. How did you find out about this call to disarm?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard this call to disarm over the local radio, Radio Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it, as the order says here, all paramilitary formations and individuals, that was said over the radio, should surrender their arms?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that aimed at everyone or a specific element of the population?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No it doesn't. I'm going to ask for why he says it or how he knows what he's about to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection rejected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that aimed at all or just certain sections of the population?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This call was aimed at the Bosniak and Croatian population only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because in that period, within the unit of the Yugoslav People's Army that was in that area, there were only members of the Serb people. According to the decision passed by the Crisis Staff, it was the legal and legitimate unit in that area. Also, at the public security station, in the police, there were only members of the Serb people who were left. In the opinion of the Crisis Staff, it was legal and legitimate too. It was the legal and legitimate unit. So this only pertained to the Bosniak and Croatian population. For the most part, those policemen, Bosniaks and Croats, who had stopped working, who were forced to stop working at the police station in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What effect did that call to disarm have on you and the other members of the non-Serbs whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This propaganda or rather this call that was broadcast over Radio Teslic introduced quite a bit of panic among the Bosniak and Croat populations. They were trying to fathom what this meant. A number of them returned their hunting weapons or the pistols that they had obtained legally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Amongst the Serbs that you knew, did this call cause any of the panic that it caused to the Bosniaks and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm going to object again, Your Honour, I think that calls for speculation of what other people felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not speculation at all. It's a perception that he may have arrived at, having been present and having experienced these events. So it's not speculation. Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did this panic that you've described, people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from this, this is a question that has been repeatedly asked actually to about 80 or 90 per cent of the witnesses that have come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Talked about the panic it caused, people handing in not illegal weapons but legal weapons. The people, the Serbs that you knew, did they have the same panic, handing in weapons that were legally permitted?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They did not feel this kind of panic and they were not handing in their weapons either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself possess any weapon?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that a pistol for which you had a permit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got that pistol legally from the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence, and I had a permit for that weapon in my official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hand in your pistol?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that? Or rather why didn't you hand it in?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid for my own safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you think might happen, as far as you or your family were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was in Teslic then with my wife and our eight-month-old child, we were alone in our apartment, and the only kind of safety I could fear after everything that had happened at the police station, was that I had this pistol. If my apartment were to be attacked or broken into or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that everything that had happened at the police station. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: What I already said, at the police station there were only ethnic Serb policemen left. I did not trust the police station in Teslic any longer either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to think that there might be an attack on your apartment or your family?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly, I was afraid, amidst this chaos that started to prevail throughout town, also there was such lawlessness in the municipality, and in the police. People were being forced to sign a loyalty oath to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You simply no longer had an institution to rely upon and that you could expect to protect you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any information, whether right or wrong, that might suggest that you -- would be a target of any attack?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, what was the information?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: What we already touched upon, the Crisis Staff. I received information that the Crisis Staff was meeting very often and that they had compiled certain lists of Bosniaks and Croats that should particularly be paid attention to, and that should particularly be monitored.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from whom or how did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my friends in Teslic still had some contacts with ethnic Serbs that were correct. They had conveyed such information to them. Some were told quite openly that they were on such and such a list. Some were told that it would be best for them to move out of the municipality of Teslic, and it is through them that I received this type of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the lists that were compiled for Bosniaks and Croats that should be paid special attention to, were they told what was going to happen to people on this lists or what might happen to people on this lists -- on these lists?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was what?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were told quite openly that on this list were Bosniaks and Croats that the Crisis Staff planned to liquidate at a given point in time, that a certain number of Bosniaks and Croats from that list would be brought in, interrogated, mistreated, a certain number from this list would be expelled, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you speak to Mr. Peresic about this? Or if not you personally, people on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In May, I was practically no longer seeing the president of the assembly. Afterwards, there were certain initiatives that a certain number of people should start talks with the president of the assembly and the commander of the town's defence, in order to discuss possible peaceful solutions that would be acceptable to all the peoples and ethnic groups in the territory of the municipality of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did those -- did that get anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we were in a situation that gave us no way out, as far as the municipality of Teslic was concerned, in the talks we suggested that a group of prominent citizens who did not belong to any political parties, consisting of ethnic Bosniaks and Croats, should go and see the president of the municipal assembly, Mr. Peresic, and that this meeting should also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be attended by Dejan Bilanovic. An open discussion should be held, in terms of what the Bosniak and Croat population of the municipality of Teslic should do, in order to prevent anything bad for happening in the municipality of Teslic, and in order to have peace prevail there. Regrettably, this yielded no results whatsoever. Those who attended this meeting told me that the president and the commander, Dejan Bilanovic, did not really give any reason for optimism, but that certain measures would be taken within the municipality of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look very briefly, please, as an exhibit, P1953. This is a document written in September, 1993, reporting on the period between September, 1991 and September, 1993. It's a report by the SJB in Teslic. I just want to ask you about certain things that it says. It talks about, if we look halfway down, we can see reporting the joining -- Teslic on the 6th of April, joining the Krajina autonomous region, and that the Teslic public security station became part of the Banja Luka CSB. Before that, had it fallen under the Doboj CSB?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I think we see the reserve police stations mobilised. Then this paragraph, "Serbs in position of authority and some of the active duty police helped in withdrawing weapons and equipment from military depots and storing them at locations in certain villages. The vehicles carrying the weapons were escorted and guarded by the police in the RSMs" - whatever that may be - "This was one of the ways in which the SDS was helped in its work and a preparation of the Serbian people for self-defence." Were you informed by Mr. Peresic or anyone that this is what -- they or the Serbs in position of authority were doing?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then we see, after the separation of the MUP, one Croat and one Muslim pledged loyalty to the Serbian MUP. Then we see the sealing of the town. Then this incident, on the 17th of April, 1992, a group of unidentified persons threw a hand grenade at the police employees manning the checkpoint. And it goes on. Did you hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What effect did that have on how the non-Serb population, including yourself, felt about how things were going to turn out in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, this incident that had happened aggravated the situation and increased tensions among ethnic groups in Teslic. Bosniaks and Croats, as I've already said, felt to be in dire straits, as if there was no light at the end of the tunnel, and they could not expect any help or support from those institutions that according to the constitution and law were in charge of helping them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you can give the document back. Now, around the middle of May, did you hear the sounds of artillery?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did those sounds come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those sounds, the artillery sounds, came from the area of Teslic municipality where Bosniak and Croat villages were, those villages were Komusina, Slatina, Rajseva and Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly how far away were they from where you lived in the Stenjak area?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly 8 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how could you tell that it was artillery?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had served in the Yugoslav People's Army and I was an artilleryman. I was a mortar -- a member of the mortar crew, so I could easily tell those sounds apart. I could easily recognise the artillery sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you knew -- sorry, I'll change that question. Was there media reporting about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did the media say was happening?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Radio Teslic had already been taken over by Serbs, and according to Radio Teslic, strong HOS forces were concentrated in that area, together with the Green Berets, and according to those reports, the Serb armed forces were carrying out operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you accept that explanation, that this was effectively an attack or a gathering of the HOS, who were I think the Croatian forces, and the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Up to mid-May, the locals used to come from those areas to the town of Teslic. I spoke to them and they would tell me that in those areas there were just local villagers who were trying to organise their own defence in case they were to be attacked by the so-called Yugoslav People's Army and other paramilitary units. So I had first-hand knowledge on what was going on in this area that was under the blockade by the JNA and paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After this attack or whatever one likes to call it, did people try and leave the municipality? Non-Serbs, I should add.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Panic increased amongst Bosniaks and Croats in Teslic and in other parts of the municipality so that already during that period, people started moving out or fleeing on a larger scale, people who were fleeing were Bosniaks and Croats, and they were running to the neighbouring municipality of Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened if the authorities caught the people who were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The only road that one could take from Teslic was not even a road but a route through the woods towards Tesanj. In that area, there were already paramilitary Serbian formations which would intercept citizens, search them, mistreat them, and if they were on the lists that were compiled by the Crisis Staff, then they would be returned to Teslic. If not, they would be allowed to proceed towards Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was happening to the people who were returned to Teslic? Were they allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, did you and others decide -- you and your family and others, decide to leave?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you take the decision that you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already given us an answer to that earlier on when you were asking him about the personal danger that he was perceiving.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was why he kept his pistol, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it went beyond that. Any way, if you want to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I may as well get the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's mentioned that he had a wife and an eight-month-old baby.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the final, if you like, thing or combination of circumstances that made you decide to leave?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: On that evening, that is on the 26th of May, two or three tanks stormed into Teslic. Those were JNA tanks. This increased the panic among the citizens and I finally took the decision to flee Teslic and go towards Tesanj. I have to be honest and say that I did not expect that concentration camps would ever be open in Teslic. I did not expect that there would be cruel killings. As one of the leaders of the SDA, I primarily feared that I would be interrogated by the Serbian police in Teslic, that I would be mistreated and that this mistreatment would be more of a psychological nature but later on, when I heard what had happened in Teslic to the Croats and the Bosniaks who had remained there, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I found it very difficult to accept that things like that could ever have happened in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so on the 26th of May, did yourself and others in fact go through the woods and went to Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked my friend, Ibro Merjamic, who was a villager of Stenjak, the neighbouring village of Tesanj, I asked him to try and take me through the woods to Tesanj. If you take this route through the woods it would take about an hour and a half. The ten of us led by this friend of mine travelled for six hours to Tesanj. We crossed various streams and we managed to avoid those paramilitary formations that had been stationed along that forest road from Teslic to Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And whilst you remained in Tesanj, as I think we've mentioned, did you become the Presidency of -- the president of the War Presidency of effectively Teslic in exile?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did you return to Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After all of these developments, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the -- after -- did you go back to Teslic after the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. And I don't know if -- who will be leading the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I will be, Your Honour. Is this a good time to take a break and then go straight through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I was going to suggest but I think it would be more convenient. How much time do you think you will require?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't think it will be very long, Your Honour. I do not think it will be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, if we start -- let's take a break of 25 minutes in any case. We keep it at 25 minutes and we take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Baruch? Now, Witness, I should like to draw your attention to a principle that -- a rule that you need to follow, and that we impose here, and namely that you do not have a right to make any distinction between questions coming from the Prosecution or questions coming from the Defence. The accused here, personally or through his lawyers, has a right o cross-examine each witness what is brought forward and that necessarily entails a responsibility, an obligation, on your part to answer each question that is put to you from the -- from the Defence as fully and as truthfully as you can. In conformity with the solemn declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony. You are going to be cross-examined by Madam Baruch. Madam Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, I'm one of the lawyers for Mr. Brdjanin. I'm going to ask you a few questions. The first is I'd like to try to understand your participation in the organisation of the SDA. I believe that you mentioned that in your statement that you were -- that you participated in the formation. Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the president of the initiative committee to establish the SDA in Teslic. Once we were aware of the fact that general and democratic multi-party elections would be held in Yugoslavia, we set out to establish new political organisations, so I decided to become one of the initiators to establish the SDA in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And I noticed as well in your statement, or rather your statement here today, that you are the vice-president of the Republika Srpska. Did I understand that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And are you the only vice-president or is there more than one vice-president?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There are two vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the ethnicity of the other vice-president is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the constitutional amendments, one vice-president is a Bosniak and the other one is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So that in the Republika Srpska, all three ethnicities are represented in high positions; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And can you tell me if you're also a minister or a secretary of any sort or is your sole position that of one of the vice-presidents of the RS?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not hold a position in the government of Republika Srpska. According to the constitution, the Republika Srpska has a president and president has its two vice-presidents, that means I do not hold any positions in the government of Republika Srpska itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, I think you haven't testified about this but other people may have mentioned similar situations. I think that there was a bit of a hoorah recently, that is after the year 2000, when you visited some grave exhumations for Muslims who were killed during 1991 and 1992; is that correct? Was there some protestations about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any protests. Can you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Fine. I was trying to find out if anybody was disturbed because you visited the exhumations, if there were any Serb protests about that, because, in fact, I think it's perfectly reasonable for you to visit the scene of an exhumation and show your respect. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present during the burial of the exhumed remains of the people of Srebrenica, and this has recently taken place in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And you did not do that as any provocative or inappropriate activity on your part, did you? You were merely showing your respect and your concern to people of your ethnicity; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That burial unfortunately was attended by the officials of Republika Srpska who are Muslims. We would have liked to see the president and the other vice-president at that burial. I attended as one of the vice-presidents of Republika Srpska. I was invited, as such, by the organisers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this would be an appropriate point to remind you to listen carefully to my questions because we can go a whole lot faster if you answer the specific question that I ask. Now, you said that you had some conversations with Mr. Peresic, who was the president of the Teslic Municipal Assembly, and I think you told us that Mr. Peresic was a member of the SDS. Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The reason that I'm asking that, Mr. Osmanovic, is because I've heard that he was a member and maybe even is still a member of the SDP party. Have you ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the League of Communists in the former Yugoslavia before the elections that took place in November, 1990. After that, he was a member of the SDS, as far as I know he was never a member of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Is that because you considered him a member of the SDS or because you know some specific fact situation associating him with the SDS and not the SDP?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party and he was on its list for municipal deputies. He was on the SDS list. He represented the SDS as one of its candidates for the deputies in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I referred you to conversations that you reported having with Mr. Peresic, and one of those conversations was with regard to why Serbs did not want to leave Yugoslavia, and become part of a new, independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember being asked about that when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mr. Peresic told you that the Serbs did not want to find themselves a minority in an independent Bosnia controlled by Muslims and Croats? Did he indicate that to you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, when the JNA came to the town of Teslic to take the reserve military records, you've told us generally that the people of the town prevented them from doing it on the first occasion. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was that all citizens of every ethnicity in Teslic prevented him from doing that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said preventing him; I meant preventing the JNA. Thank you for understanding my question. So, can you tell me how these citizens of every ethnicity from Teslic that prevented the taking of the reserve list, military reserve lists, can you tell me how they were able to block the army of their country?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the news spread in Teslic that the officers of the JNA had arrived in the Secretariat for National Defence in order to take over the records -- and before that, we heard on the television that such things had already happened in other municipalities, the civilians had already been informed about that and what was happening with the records. After that, there was a spontaneous rally of the city population in Teslic municipality, and as I've already told you, they prevented the JNA from doing what they wanted to do. They threw themselves in front of the vehicles of the JNA and the building of the Secretariat for National Defence was blocked by the bodies of these people. There was also the police there, members of the public security station were there, so the whole situation bordered on an incident, an incident was threatening to escalate from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did any of the citizens arm themselves for that event, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And you said -- by the way, you said that the next -- that night or the next night, the JNA was able to get the information from the People's Defence headquarters because you believe there was a Serb employee on duty that night? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he said it already. He did say it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you is wasn't the head of the People's Defence at that time a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in the Secretariat, after regular working hours, there had to be persons on duty, and everybody who was employed at the Secretariat had their turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. But assignments were made by the head of that department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The secretary of the Secretariat still abided by the principle that there had to be a roster as to when who would be on duty, irrespective of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And that was the man, Degirmendzic; is that right? Mensur Degirmendzic? Is that right? He was head of the department?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You also talked about later there were about a hundred soldiers, headed by Veljko Bosanac, stationed at Djulici -- I hope I'm pronouncing that in a way that you can understand it. Do you remember the month of that assignment?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And was that the time that JNA troops were leaving Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So that the JNA troops who had previously been stationed in Slovenia or Croatia would have to find another place to be stationed, correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In a certain sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were saying that now it happened that 100 JNA soldiers - and they were JNA soldiers at that time - were stationed in Teslic municipality, "they never gave us an explanation," who would you have expected to give you an explanation with regard to the JNA forces' assignments?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We expected the president of the assembly to convene all the persons in charge in the municipality, the head of the public security station, the chief of police, this Major Bosanac, and to seek information in this regard. It was to be expected that this would be dealt with by a session of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And in fact, what had occurred is JNA headquarters had -- in Belgrade, had ordered the assignment of those JNA troops to Teslic municipality; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as for conditions for a longer stay of these JNA units, there weren't any in the local commune of Djulici, in this make-shift barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So is what you just told me that the barracks that they were actually stationed at, in, were not designed to be permanent barracks but merely almost the temporary make-shift place for them to stay? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But you used the word "make-shift."

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a military facility that was used when there was mobilisation in Doboj, Teslic, and even beyond. This is where reservists stayed for a certain amount of time. So these are prefabricated buildings. That's why I used the word.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And in amongst those hundred soldiers, were there any Bosniaks in that unit? That is, people of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Osmanovic. I think you just said you don't know instead of guessing, and thank you, I hope you can continue to do that. It's very helpful to the Court. You said in your statement that there was even an area where they trained nearby. Would you agree with me that it is useful and regular for soldiers to continue their training periodically and that there is nothing suspicious about soldiers training?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there were reservists at that training.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim reservists at that training?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Is that because the Muslim reservists had refused mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said in your statement that, "We learned that their presence was to arm the Serbian civilian population." Can you tell me who learned that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We received that information from our local people who were moving around in that area. This area is populated by Serbs only, so these citizens of ours had received information from citizens who were of Serb ethnicity as to what had been going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So is what you're telling the Court what you learned was not directly from any official source but you heard it from someone who heard it from somebody else who was just moving around in the area and gleaning information? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously, nobody felt it was necessary to provide anybody else with official information, anybody who was in position of authority from among the Bosniaks and the Croats in the municipality of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So people who you knew, Muslims in Teslic, getting pieces of information from Serbs in that area where there were no Muslims, discussed this amongst themselves and that's how you learned the purpose of the JNA being there? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. Until then, the training of reservists had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. never taken place in that way in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And in fact, you had not had JNA stationed in that particular area in the past; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Prosecutor asked you to look at P1925 and I would like you to look at that document again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I didn't prepare a list because I didn't know which documents Ms. Korner was going to use and I see that the bailiff has those records easily available.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So Mr. Osmanovic, could you look specifically at the second page of that agenda item? Because you drew a conclusion with regard to Prosecutor's Exhibit 1925 and specifically paragraph 1.8. I think you'll agree that I'm reading this correctly when I say it says, "All paramilitary formations and individuals illegally possessing arms" and you can read the rest of those sentences. It does say that even in B/C/S, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You don't need to answer it because the Prosecution agrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, the reason that I directed your attention to that is because I believe you had indicated in your direct examination that the paramilitaries in the area were Serb paramilitaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: There were paramilitaries who were Muslim in the area of Teslic, inside the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As you said, this referred to all paramilitary formations, and it was addressed by the Crisis Staff of Teslic and there were no Bosniaks or Croats on the Crisis Staff. They thought that the present units of the Yugoslav People's Army along with the reservists who were undergoing training were legal and legitimate forces in the territory of the municipality of Teslic. They also considered the public security station and its policemen to be legal and legitimate. In their view, this call referred to the Bosniak and Croat population only.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, I did not ask what somebody's internal thinking process and what their view may have been. My question to you was with regard to the paramilitary organisations operating within the Teslic municipality. Can't you agree with me that there were Serb paramilitary organisations operating within the Teslic municipality? There were such paramilitaries, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the wording of this agenda item, 1.8, doesn't limit itself to certain paramilitary organisations, and I'll get back to that in a minute. It says all paramilitary formations, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you raised a question in my mind. Were there, to your knowledge, Muslim, Bosniak, paramilitary operatives in the municipality of Teslic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, in the territory of the municipality of Teslic, there was self-organisation among the Bosniak and Croat populations in certain villages only. That is to say, to put up resistance if they are attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking in May of 1992, about paramilitary organisations in Teslic that were Bosniak or Muslim, whom you have described as self-organisation; is that right? When you use self-organisation, you mean they formed paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: To put it in a certain way, this was defence of Bosniak and Croat villages. That is to say self-organisation on the part of that section of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mrs. Baruch. It's my impression that you're trying to answer this question tangentially. The question is a very simple one and a very direct one. Do you see any distinction at all in your mind between what has been referred to you as a paramilitary organisation and what you have described as self-organisation for the purposes of defence? It's being suggested to you that these are one and the same thing, paramilitaries and self-organised groups. Would you agree with that proposition or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the Bosniak and the Croat population was completely pushed out of the police, out of the Yugoslav People's Army that was present in Teslic. They embarked upon this form of self-defence only if the police and these units went and attacked their villages. Somebody can consider that to be defence or a way of self-organisation in case of an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's as far as you're going to get, Mrs. Baruch, so move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I suspect the Court is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You have talked before about people who were acting in a way to defend themselves because the Bosniaks were no longer a part of the police and had refused mobilisation, and you talked about that when Ms. Korner referred you to P1953. And you can tell me if you need that document again, but it's a very small piece that I'm referring to, because -- and I'll read that to you. It says, "The enemy forces could not resign themselves to do this and the first to come under attack were the members of the Serbian MUP. In the evening of April 17th, 1992, a group of unidentified persons threw a hand grenade at the police employees manning the Margita checkpoint." Those people manning that checkpoint were Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the unidentified persons who threw a hand gun -- a hand grenade at the police employees, you would agree that they were non-Serbs; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot agree. I don't know. There never had been a definite investigation in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, either they were Serbs throwing grenades at Serbs, in which case some Serbs had illegal weapons, or they were non-Serbs throwing a grenade at Serbs, in which case there were non-Serbs having an illegal weapon, and so directing your attention again back to P1925, when, on the agenda item, it said, "All paramilitary formations and individuals illegally possessing arms and ammunition are called upon to hand them over to the municipal TO," and so that section of the agenda was directed at all citizens, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason that I direct you back to P1925 again is that you felt that by reading it, you could explain that it was only directed at Serbs and Croats because the police were legally armed and the TO was legally armed, but there were people in Teslic who were illegally armed at that time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, this is the first time I see this document. Unfortunately, I was not made aware of it before that, but certainly there were people in Teslic who were in the possession of weapons, illegally and legally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And as well, you heard over the radio, over the radio, an announcement that all people in Teslic should turn in their illegal weapons; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that there was never any resistance to the Serbs, and a portion of citizens turned in their weapons. But I've heard you talk today about resistance to authorities. I've heard you say today that there were people who had illegal weapons, and there were Muslims who self-organised for groups that you described as, to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, that's a mistake, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm sorry, if that's suggested that wasn't in the statement, it's actually in the statement. If Ms. Baruch has a look at page 8, she will see there is a paragraph which begins: "There was never any resistance --" and if she reads on it says, "Villagers in the Teslic municipality were less likely to turn in their weapons and there was some organisation of these villagers into defence forces for their areas but eventually, I think, almost every one turned in their weapon."

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Osmanovic, that there was resistance in Teslic, such as the throwing of the hand grenade at the police? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no resistance in terms of carrying out this order or proclamation of the Crisis Staff. A significant number of citizens, particularly in town, returned the weapons that they had had legally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, I understand that what you're saying that people who were law-abiding citizens, who had registered their guns and had them legally were also turning in their weapons; is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that in the territory of the municipality of Teslic, there were many things that were going on that were not in accordance with the law so this was not in accordance with the law but many people handed over their weapons, primarily Bosniaks and Croats, because they wanted a peaceful solution to be found within the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you know that there were searches of homes for illegal weapons? Do you know that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was in the territory of the municipality of Teslic, there were no searches of homes for weapons. Later on, according to the information that I received while I was in Tesanj, such things did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you hear that a police officer was killed when a grenade exploded that had been set up as a trap while they were searching a home for illegal weapons? Did you learn that while you were in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You've talked about a list of people to be watched. Have you ever seen a -- such a written list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You have seen that list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I only saw that list once the Dayton Accords were signed. It was published in the newspapers, on the territory of Republika Srpska. It was published in an independent newspaper, and that was something that was not good for editor of that paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: It was published in the Republika Srpska, in which newspaper, please?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: An independent newspaper, whose owner was a journalist Kopanja. After this article, that was published over a few issues, he had his car blown up and he was severely injured as a result of that. He became disabled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you tell me when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the name of the newspaper, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we have a lot of information about that, rather than asking the witness to try and remember, we can provide the name of the newspaper and the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can I get some idea of the date now, Your Honour, if he knows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is a well-known thing when this happened. It was either in 1999 or 2000. This newspaper confirmed all the information that we had previously received. My name was also in that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: It was a list of names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, you talked in your statement about some violence occurring regarding the Muslim, Albanian pastry shop. And I think you told us today that there was a mechanism for putting things on the agenda at the Teslic municipality. Did you attempt to put that matter on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And was it voted to be placed on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipal assembly was of the opinion that this should not have been put on the agenda. He thought that the discussion on the political and security situation in Teslic could aggravate the tensions among the deputies. He as the person who was in charge of proposing items for the agenda, thought this should not have been put often the agenda. The deputies who belonged to my political party did raise this issue but we could never obtain a qualified majority in favour of putting this on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you just help me with one thing, then? Was -- am I correctly remembering that the SDA -- I'm sorry, SDS, had 48 per cent of the municipal assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So the majority of people were not SDS. The majority of the people were the coalition of other parties that made up the other 52 per cent; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a captious question, Madam Baruch. You're using the word coalition. No one suggested that the remaining 52 per cent was coalesced or had a coalition in operation between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the question suggested it, I can rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So the other 52 per cent of the assembly -- at least 3 per cent of them agreed with the president of the assembly that it should not get on the agenda; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: A parliamentary majority, or the coalition in Teslic, was made up of the SDS, the HDZ and the SDA. That was the majority. When the SDA deputies proposed that this should be put on the agenda, this could not be done without the deputies of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I thought that you had instructed us today that any item could be put on the agenda by a majority vote. Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And that 48 per cent of the deputies were SDS. I've got that right as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So if the other deputies who were not SDS, who agreed that it should go on the agenda, it could have gotten on the agenda; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: But there were SDS -- there were Serb representatives in other parties, like the SDP, the reformists, and some Serbian deputies were not supportive of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put the question straight and clear. Those who had an interest to have this included in the agenda, were they in the majority or in a minority at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the voting, it turned out that they were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. And one other thing. I thought I read that the commander of the police was a man by the name of Ferid Mahalbasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Was the commander of the police a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Because I may have said his name wrong or picked the wrong name. Okay. So when something would have to be investigated at that time, there was at least a commander of the police who would have input into the investigation, at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to complement this, according to him in his statement, and I think he did repeat that earlier on today, the commander of the police was Sabahudin Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While the chief of public security was Dusan Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So when an investigation had to be done early on there was a Bosniak who had input into such investigations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the law, this should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And do you know who was the commander of the police when that Muslim-Albanian pastry shop suffered an explosion?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And his name, please?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sabahudin Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The name that I mentioned before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the name of Ferid Mahalbasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: It was Sabahudin Mehmedovic. And he was the commander at the time that the Albanian shop exploded and he had at least some input into the investigation of that event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He complained to me that his work was obstructed, that there was nothing whatsoever he could do with that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, do you know that there was any information gathered as to who had done that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. On page 6 of your statement, you said that in April of 1992, the Teslic municipal authority met to discuss the joining of the municipality to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you weren't informed of that, and you said despite the fact that you believed the meeting was statutorily illegal, despite that they met, after getting orders from Pale?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To be accurate, he didn't say he believed it was statutorily illegal. He said that it was statutorily illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, she is right, but he said so because he believed so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Despite that you indicate they met after getting orders from Pale. Tell me about that. How do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I talked about the way the Municipal Assembly of Teslic should have worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I thought we had a deal that I would -- you would try to answer my question, okay? And my question really goes to the orders from Pale. So can you tell me how you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This way of calling the sessions of the municipal assembly should have been preceded by instructions from a centre, and I also learned about that from my friends who had good relations with the Serbs who were employed in municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be the last question for today. Do you have much longer, Mrs. Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I never like to promise a court because I try to be as honest as I can. I cannot promise it would be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we finish with the witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only on the question of Mr. Sebire, I understand from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I was coming to that actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- from Ms. Baruch, that Mr. Ackerman's, I don't know if consent is the right word, but acquiescence to the plan to call Mr. Sebire on Friday, he is happy for him to be called in chief but would prefer cross-examination to be adjourned in which case, Your Honour, we are, subject to Your Honour we are content with that. We would ask that the cross-examination occur on Tuesday, the 10th of June, because of problems of getting a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Is that the original scheduled date?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was the original scheduled date for him to be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, and Mr. Ackerman was very pleased with the compromise of the court. Thank you for suggesting it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how it will be. Mr. Sebire will attend -- come over on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He comes down, in fact, Your Honour, as opposed to over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the examination-in-chief. Cross-examination will be held in the course of the sitting of the 10th of June. We are now handing down a decision on documents 1937, 1940, 1950. Our decision is: Having looked at the documents and in conformity with the previous decision and the practice of this Tribunal, that we cannot -- that there is nothing on the face of these documents that a priori would make it incumbent on this Tribunal to declare them inadmissible at this stage so they are -- they are being admitted with the usual caveat that the probative value will be assigned to them as we go along, depending on what the evidence will be on them, as well as on other matters. The last thing is we had discussed very, very briefly, although I did get an indication that this would not materialise but I want to make sure, we had discussed sometime last week the possibility of working extended hours next week. The week of the 2nd to the 6th. Which we are very well prepared to do, in order to try and recover some lost time. I know that Mr. Ackerman should be back amongst us next week. Are you in a position to enlighten us on this matter, Mrs. Baruch

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I would ask this Court, I would implore this Court that if we have to catch up time, perhaps we can do it later on but that will be his first week back here. In additionally I have a question, we have not been informed that we have a new case manager but the Court stated something to that effect yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was informally informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So we should expect some kind of a decision communicated to us soon but as the Court knows, at this time we are working without somebody who speaks B/C/S in the team. So that communicating with our client has to be scheduled in advance and so I would ask not, please not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as Your Honour knows, we are anxious that if we have to try and complete our case by the 1st of August, that we sit as much as possible. But clearly, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Mrs. Baruch has said deserves understanding. And I think for the time being, we will forget about sitting extended hours next week. And we'll take the matter up again as we go along. Please try tomorrow to ensure that we finish with this witness so that he can return home and we can start with Mr. Sebire on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, while you've just dealt with the exhibits, very quickly just so Your Honours can make a note of Exhibit P1942 and for this reason. Your Honour will recall that in other exhibits, there has been a query about who this man Milos was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it was mentioned by one witness. Milos was identified by one witness before we broke --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Maybe I missed it but anyhow there is a clear indication however, that whoever was using the pseudonym Milos was an employee of the SMB, which was the security services. But you will remember right at the beginning there was a lot of discussion about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And I think also we are told that it was a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. It's an operative name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the witness who said it, to be frank with you, I don't remember. So that's it. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. And that will be a usual sitting right through 1.45. Thank you and have a nice day.
